content.overview: Section 46 provides that a certificate issued under the common seal, if any, of the company or signed by two directors or by a director and the company secretary, specifying the shares held by any person, is prima facie evidence of the title of the person to such shares. The section also addresses duplicate certificates and prescribed manner and form.
content.glance: Share certificate is prima facie evidence of title; issued under seal or signed as prescribed; duplicate certificates on conditions; prescribed form and manner.
content.study: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 46 (Certificate of shares). A share certificate issued under the company's common seal, if any, or signed by two directors or by a director and the company secretary, specifying the shares held by a person, is prima facie evidence of that person's title to the shares. For securities held in a depository, the depository's record is prima facie evidence. A duplicate certificate may be issued where the original is proved lost or destroyed, or where it is defaced, mutilated or torn and surrendered, subject to the prescribed form, evidence, fee and indemnity terms. A certificate may not be issued in duplicate without the statutory safeguards and applicable rules. If a company, with intent to defraud, issues a duplicate certificate, the company is punishable with a fine of at least five times the face value of the shares involved, extendable to ten times that face value or ₹10 crore, whichever is higher; every officer in default is liable under section 447. Certificate-delivery timelines after allotment or transfer are separately addressed in section 56(4).

sections.heading: Evidentiary effect
sections.body: A properly issued certificate specifying the shares held is prima facie evidence of the holder's title. For dematerialised securities, the depository record is prima facie evidence.

sections.heading: Duplicate certificate
sections.body: A duplicate may be issued if the original is proved lost/destroyed or is defaced, mutilated or torn and surrendered, subject to prescribed form, evidence, fee and indemnity requirements.

sections.heading: Fraudulent duplicate
sections.body: Where the company issues a duplicate certificate with intent to defraud, the company is punishable with a fine of at least five times the face value of the shares involved, extendable to ten times that face value or ₹10 crore, whichever is higher; every officer in default is liable under section 447.

sections.heading: Distinct certificate-delivery deadline
sections.body: Section 46 concerns certificate evidentiary effect and duplicates. Delivery deadlines after allotment, transfer or transmission are separately governed by section 56(4).

examples.title: Valid certificate
examples.body: A certificate signed by two directors specifying the member’s shares is prima facie evidence of that member’s title under s. 46.

examples.title: Lost certificate
examples.body: A member proves loss of the original certificate and seeks a duplicate. The Board may issue a duplicate on terms as to evidence, indemnity and fee.

hypotheticals.question: A company issues a duplicate share certificate with intent to defraud. What penalty applies?
hypotheticals.analysis: The company faces a fine of at least five times the face value of the shares involved, extendable to ten times that face value or ₹10 crore, whichever is higher. Every officer in default is liable under section 447.

hypotheticals.question: Does a share certificate conclusively determine every dispute about ownership?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 46 gives a qualifying certificate prima facie evidentiary effect; it is not expressed as conclusive proof of every underlying dispute.

distinctions.title: Share certificate and certificate delivery
distinctions.left: Section 46 governs evidentiary effect and duplicate certificates.
distinctions.right: Section 56(4) governs deadlines for delivering certificates after incorporation, allotment, transfer/transmission or debenture allotment.

rows.left: Prima facie evidence and fraud penalty

misconceptions.trap: Treating a share certificate as conclusive proof of all ownership issues.
misconceptions.correction: Section 46 says prima facie evidence of title.

misconceptions.trap: Issuing a duplicate without proving loss/destruction or surrender of a damaged original and meeting prescribed safeguards.
misconceptions.correction: Apply the statutory grounds and current rules for duplicate certificates.

misconceptions.trap: Using the former general fine instead of the current fraudulent-duplicate provision.
misconceptions.correction: For intent-to-defraud duplicate issue, state the amended face-value-linked fine and section 447 liability.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What is the evidentiary effect of a share certificate?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: It is prima facie evidence of title to the shares specified; a depository record is prima facie evidence for dematerialised holdings.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What is the current penalty for a fraudulent duplicate certificate?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Company fine of at least five times the face value of the shares involved, extendable to ten times that face value or ₹10 crore, whichever is higher; every officer in default is liable under section 447.
